ALUSI-FULL:v15p215/r2.claim: On al-Khafaji's reading, revelation makes the sleepers' case visible, reassuring believers and cutting off deniers' arguments; the wording points to the implication of knowledge suited to context.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p215/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p215/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p215/r3.claim: The duration dispute is singled out because disagreement over it gives the story stronger public visibility and wider circulation.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p215/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p215/r4.speaker: الكشف
ALUSI-FULL:v15p215/r4.claim: Al-Kashf explains knowledge as figurative distinction and disclosure: the people who know the duration are exposed, though neither party actually did so.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p215/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p215/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p215/r5.claim: The author finds al-Kashf's explanation less costly than al-Khafaji's and prefers the test-like illustration; the worry about implying divine desire is negligible.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p215/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p215/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p215/r6.claim: In the active reading liyaʿlama, God is the subject and an object is omitted; the following clause supplies two objects, or one if knowledge means recognition.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p215/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p215/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p215/r7.claim: A passive reading liyaʿlama omits its deputy subject; the following clause may supply the objects or the single object according to the sense of knowledge.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p215/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p215/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p215/r8.claim: Some Kufans allow the following clause itself to function as the deputy subject; Basrans forbid clauses as subjects or deputy subjects, while Kufans differ about the condition for allowing it.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p258/r9.claim: The two groups' dispute over the duration signifies return from spiritual intoxication to sobriety, subsistence after annihilation, or disclosure after retreat; the latter pair are close interpretations.

ELMALILI:18:10-12/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:10-12/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:10-12/r2.claim: God's saying that He might know means bringing the matter to manifestation and making it clear, so that the youths themselves understand.

ELMALILI:18:10-12/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:10-12/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:10-12/r3.claim: The two parties are the monotheist believing Companions of the Cave and their polytheist opponents.

ELMALILI:18:10-12/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:10-12/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:10-12/r4.claim: On waking, the youths saw that they had succeeded in their undertaking and goals and had attained divine mercy.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p268/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p268/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p268/r7.claim: Baʿath means awakening them from sleep; the metaphor of rousing a camel also hints at resurrection, the story’s central proof of its possibility and manner.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p268/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p268/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p268/r8.claim: One proposed reading makes the two parties factions among the sleepers, but Ibn Ashur finds it remote because one person asks and they were not trying to calculate their sleep duration.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p268/r9.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p268/r9.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p268/r9.claim: He instead understands the parties as townspeople who later disagreed about how long the sleepers had remained in the cave, one group estimating correctly and another incorrectly.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r1.claim: The parties should not be read as groups among the sleepers: the questioner and respondents are differentiated, and the sleepers were not undertaking a count.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r2.claim: Making God’s knowledge the purpose of awakening indirectly signals that people differed over the duration; divine knowledge of actual events may be termed tanjīzī attachment in kalām even before an event occurs.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r3.speaker: الزمخشري
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r3.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī, following Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī, reads aḥṣā as a finite past verb to avoid the rare, nonanalogical formation of an elative from a quadriliteral.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r4.speaker: الزجاج
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r4.claim: Al-Zajjāj chooses the second parsing, taking aḥṣā as an elative adjective formed from a quadriliteral.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r5.claim: Despite its irregularity, the elative is common in eloquent Arabic and the Qur’an; aḥṣā means more exact and accurate counting that matches reality rather than guesswork.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r6.claim: Ayy is an interrogative subject suspending li-naʿlama, aḥṣā is its predicate, and amadan is a specification of the comparative relation, as in ‘more wealth than me.’

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p269/r7.claim: The episode exposes how people’s chronologies of events become inconsistent guesses, revealing widespread negligence in dating and defining historical events.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#3/r10.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#3/r10.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#3/r10.claim: Amad is a duration with an unknown but bounded endpoint, while abad is unlimited; amad focuses on an endpoint whereas zamān can span beginning and end.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#3/r11.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#3/r11.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#3/r11.claim: Amad differs from zamān by considering a duration's endpoint, while zamān can encompass both its beginning and endpoint.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#3/r12.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#3/r12.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#3/r12.claim: God's knowledge here is actual manifestation of an event in its particular existence.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#3/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#3/r3.speaker: الراغب
TABATABAI:18:9-26#3/r3.claim: Al-Rāghib defines ḥizb as a substantial group.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#3/r9.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#3/r9.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#3/r9.claim: Baʿth here means waking them, not resurrection, because the preceding verse describes sleep.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#32/r10.claim: The cave story circulated in detailed reports from al-Qummī, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid, Ibn Isḥāq, Wahb ibn Munabbih, and al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, among others.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r1.claim: The transmitted accounts disagree even on major features, while reports about dates, rulers, lineage, appearance, names, and the title أصحاب الرقيم diverge still more.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r2.claim: One cause is the story’s prominence among People of the Book: Quraysh learned it from them, and its Christian images and monuments spread it widely, so communities reshaped it to fit their beliefs.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r3.claim: A second cause is Muslims’ broad collection of outside reports, especially through converts such as Wahb ibn Munabbih and Kaʿb al-Aḥbār; later transmitters treated such material as prophetic reports.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#33/r4.claim: The Qurʾān selects key lessons that serve guidance instead of supplying a complete historical account; it is a book of guidance, not history.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#34/r1.claim: The Qurʾān omits names, ancestry, birth, upbringing, occupations, social standing, dates, rulers, cities, persecutors, and the dog’s identity because guidance does not depend on them; historians and early exegetes filled these gaps, producing divergent accounts.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#35/r1.claim: After 309 years God raised the youths to show how He had rescued them; they awoke disoriented, and some guessed they had slept a day or part of one while others deferred to God’s knowledge.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.speaker: أهل الرواية والتاريخ
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r1.claim: Most historians date the story between Jesus and Muḥammad; it is absent from the two Testaments, though some Muslim reports say Quraysh heard it from Jews, while Christians preserved it extensively.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#36/r2.claim: Christian accounts resemble Ibn Isḥāq’s report from Ibn ʿAbbās in some respects but differ from Muslims on the number of sleepers, whether they had a dog, and the length of their sleep.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#38/r4.claim: After centuries as a ruined, forgotten site, Jordanian excavation uncovered Rujayb; the author considers its archaeological signs and some Muslim reports the strongest fit for the Qurʾānic cave.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r1.claim: Amman stands on the site of Philadelphia, a major and beautiful city before Islam that remained under Roman control from the early second century until the Muslim conquest.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r2.claim: Other proposed locations include a cave on Mount Qāsiyūn near Damascus, one at Petra, a Scandinavian cave with seven uncorrupted Roman-looking bodies, and a cave near Nakhchivan.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#39/r3.claim: No evidence identifies any proposed cave as the Qurʾānic one; the Scandinavian and Caucasus claims conflict with the story’s Roman setting and the limits of Roman power.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#4/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#4/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#4/r1.claim: The Quran uses knowledge in the sense of actual manifestation, as in the verses about knowing who supports God and that the messengers delivered their messages.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#4/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#4/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#4/r2.claim: Some interpreters gloss the phrase as making what God already knows manifest.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#4/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#4/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#4/r3.claim: The clause gives the purpose for awakening them, with the lam marking an intended end.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#4/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#4/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#4/r4.claim: The two factions are the cave youths questioning one another after awakening; identifying them instead as believers and unbelievers among their people is remote.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#5/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#5/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#5/r1.claim: Aḥṣā is most naturally a past-tense verb, with amad as its object and the phrase about their stay restricting the duration counted.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#5/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#5/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#5/r2.claim: Reading aḥṣā as a comparative adjective and supplying an implied verb for amad is possible but strained.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#5/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#5/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#5/r3.claim: The three verses summarize their flight and prayer for rescue, their counted years of sleep, and their awakening to determine which faction counted the duration.

TABATABAI:18:9-26#5/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:9-26#5/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:9-26#5/r4.claim: Each opening verse gives one of the story's three summary elements; later verses add what happened after the people discovered them.

ASAD-NOTES:18:10#n10/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:18:10#n10/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:18:10#n10/r1.claim: The verb may instead mean sent them forth, suggesting a return to active worldly life.

ASAD-NOTES:18:10#n11/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:18:10#n11/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:18:10#n11/r1.claim: Since God knows all times, His taking cognizance means bringing an event into being and making it known to creatures, hence marking it out to the world.

ASAD-NOTES:18:10#n12/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:18:10#n12/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:18:10#n12/r1.claim: The two parties metonymically represent the viewpoints in verse 19; ahsa means comprehend, not merely calculate, because the parable concerns the spiritual meaning of elapsed time.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: These verses summarize the whole story before its details, keeping its purpose in view so secondary details do not obscure it; the Qur'an often uses this narrative pattern.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: God woke them so two groups would debate how long they slept; their guesses proved unreliable, foreshadowing how people in Barzakh will perceive their span as brief.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Just as God protected them, He awakened them so their mutual questioning would expose their inability to know the elapsed time; this expands the earlier summary.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:12/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:12/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:12/r1.claim: God’s ‘that We might know’ means bringing the event forth for people to understand, not acquiring knowledge; the reading li-yuʿlama (‘so it be known’) supports that sense.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:12/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:12/r2.speaker: müfessirler
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:12/r2.claim: One view identifies the two groups as believers and unbelievers among the Cave youths’ people.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:12/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:12/r3.speaker: müfessirler
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:12/r3.claim: A second view identifies the two groups as the Cave youths and their opponents.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:12/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:12/r4.speaker: müfessirler
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:12/r4.claim: A third view identifies the groups as the youths themselves, who disagreed about how long they had slept; verse 19 reflects their exchange.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:12/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:12/r5.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:12/r5.claim: The following verses explain in greater detail the Cave story previously summarized.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p67/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p67/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p67/r1.claim: God's prior knowledge records destiny; later knowledge brings that decree to realization and concerns recompense, while human action confirms the prior knowledge.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p67/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p67/r2.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p67/r2.claim: He reads li-na'lama ayy al-hizbayn as making clear which group knows the truth about the youths' duration, rather than implying that God learns something previously unknown.

STUDYQURAN:18:12/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:12/r1.speaker: R, Ṭs
STUDYQURAN:18:12/r1.claim: Raising the youths means awakening them from sleep.

STUDYQURAN:18:12/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:12/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:12/r2.claim: The wording that God raised them to know appears to challenge divine foreknowledge; Quranic test language can mean God tests people while already knowing the answer.

STUDYQURAN:18:12/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:12/r3.speaker: R, Ṭs
STUDYQURAN:18:12/r3.claim: The two parties may be two groups among the Companions themselves.

STUDYQURAN:18:12/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:12/r4.speaker: R
STUDYQURAN:18:12/r4.claim: Another view identifies the parties as the Companions and the kings who ruled the city.

STUDYQURAN:18:12/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:12/r5.speaker: IK
STUDYQURAN:18:12/r5.claim: A further view takes the parties to be everyone who differed over how long the youths stayed.

STUDYQURAN:18:12/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:12/r6.speaker: al-Rāzī
STUDYQURAN:18:12/r6.claim: Al-Rāzī says Sufis take the verse as evidence that saints may receive karāmāt, miracles distinct from prophetic muʿjizāt.

STUDYQURAN:18:12/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:12/r7.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:12/r7.claim: Islamic texts clearly distinguish prophetic evidentiary miracles from miracles granted to saints or friends of God.

STUDYQURAN:18:intro/r11.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:intro/r11.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:intro/r11.claim: The youths' centuries-long sleep represents an intermediate realm between life and death, analogous to the state between individual death and universal resurrection.
